errors.text: The hypothesis treats a high HCP atom count as evidence of amorphization. In FCC common-neighbor analysis, HCP-classified atoms usually mark stacking faults or partial-dislocation structures, whereas genuinely amorphous disorder should increase unclassified/other atoms and suppress crystalline RDF peaks.

The reduced-rate falsification rule is not mechanically sound: a slower rate generally provides more time for thermally activated recovery or mechanical annealing, so it does not straightforwardly predict higher hardness. The proposed interpretation also conflicts with the claim that high-rate deformation causes dislocation annihilation despite preventing recovery.

The asserted temperature-dependent decrease in stacking-fault energy, localized amorphization, Cu-assisted interfacial diffusion, material transfer, and greater-than-twofold friction increase are not established by the cited evidence.
